links.comparator_used: Outcome-label-dependent (lagging) performance monitoring such as AUROC and calibration
links.outcome: Early detection of emerging post-deployment degradation (timing relative to outcome-based monitoring)
links.effect: Input missingness was associated with lower calibration slope in every system (standardized beta -0.42 to -0.21). Data latency was associated in 3 of 4 systems (-0.35 to -0.08). Missingness and latency kept negative associations in 12/12 alternative specifications. Telemetry changes preceded or co-evolved with calibration degradation, while outcome labels lagged by 24-72 hours up to 2-8 weeks depending on system.
links.tradeoff: Associations are observational, not causal. The authors say outcome-based reassessment is still needed as confirmatory evidence, and telemetry is not an unbiased measure of clinical effectiveness.
links.quote: Label-independent operational signals, including input missingness and data latency, provided early indication of emerging fragility, whereas outcome-based monitoring was delayed by label latency and documentation processes.

links.outcome: Timing of detection of post-deployment degradation (calibration slope/intercept vs AUROC)
links.effect: Mean change from validation to the first 6 months of deployment: calibration slope -0.11 (-0.14 to -0.08) vs AUROC -0.02 (-0.03 to -0.01). Calibration changed earlier than AUROC with the 3-month definition (-0.08 vs -0.01) and the 9-month definition (-0.14 vs -0.03). In System A, early-deployment AUROC was 0.81 (validation 0.82) while calibration slope fell from 1.01 to 0.88.
links.quote: These findings indicate that discrimination metrics alone would have delayed detection of post-deployment degradation, particularly in Systems A and B, where calibration drift emerged before substantial AUROC decline.

design_hint: post-deployment drift monitoring with label-independent operational telemetry
